# Cup Day, the dead coolroom and why London has made you soft

Jonno,

You’ve now messaged me enough times about the coolroom that it’s easier to put it here and send you the link. You can read it on your little London commute with your little London coffee while complaining that twelve quid is actually quite reasonable for a sandwich.

Also, yes, this all happened while you were over there finding yourself. Convenient.

So: Cup Day. Tuesday 3 November. One hundred and forty covers booked for lunch. Set menu, three courses, which normally means everybody’s calm because we know what’s coming out and roughly when. Raff was away, so I was running it. Benny was on with me, Kev was out back, and everything was fine right up until I opened the coolroom at 6.40am and got hit with that lovely lukewarm fridge smell.

The thermometer said eleven degrees.

Eleven.

Not “a bit warm because the door’s been open”. Eleven degrees. Overnight, while we were all at home sleeping like idiots, the compressor had died and taken Cup Day lunch somewhere dark with it.

You know that feeling when you look at something and your brain just refuses to participate? I stood there holding the door open, as if fresh dining-room air was going to reverse the situation. Then I checked the thermometer again because apparently the first eleven degrees might have been a joke.

Anyway. One hundred and forty people arriving for three courses. Coolroom behaving like a cupboard. Horse race in the afternoon. Beautiful.

First call was Wally from Coldline, who gave me the deeply reassuring news that he couldn’t get to us until Wednesday and the part was coming from Sydney. Excellent. I told him we had service in a few hours and he made the sort of noise fridge blokes make when they’re sorry but also fundamentally unable to bend time.

Phil’s contribution was: “Just make it work, mate.”

Which, Jonno, as you know, is not a plan. That is a sentence you say immediately before leaving someone else to invent a plan. Nobody has ever repaired a compressor by making it work. You can’t put “just make it work mate” in an ice bath and serve it with affogato.

So we started shifting everything.

The two undercounters got packed so tightly you had to perform minor surgery to get a container out. The bar fridge stopped being a bar fridge and became a very small, humiliating coolroom. Anything that could be consolidated was consolidated. Anything that couldn’t was assessed with the cold-hearted efficiency of a man who had just found eleven degrees on a thermometer.

Marta from the café next door saved us by giving us half her walk-in. Not free, obviously. Marta’s a lovely person but she runs a business, not a refrigeration-based charity. We’re paying her back in croissant credit and staff meals. By my calculations I owe her approximately three weeks of feeding her entire operation. She comes over now and just looks at me like a debt collector with excellent pastry.

At one point Benny and I had to get thirty kilos of beef shin down the laneway to Marta’s. Thirty kilos. On a milk crate trolley. In the rain.

You would have absolutely lost your mind.

Not in a useful way, either. You’d have stood there giving a speech about workplace health and safety while Benny and I did all the carrying. London has made you soft. You probably haven’t lifted anything heavier than a flat white since February.

The trolley had one wheel that was already on the fence about being a wheel, and halfway down the laneway it officially resigned. Just popped off and rolled away. So there we were, in the rain, holding up thirty kilos of beef on a three-wheeled piece of shit while Cup Day lunch ticked closer. Benny didn’t even swear. He just looked at the wheel, then at me, then started dragging.

That’s when you know service people are cooked: total equipment failure and everyone’s too busy to react properly.

Kev, meanwhile, filled the old esky with ice from the servo. Fourteen bags. The bloke behind the counter asked if we were having a party.

Kev said yes.

Which, fair enough. We were hosting 140 people and slowly losing our minds. Close enough.

We lost about eighteen hundred bucks’ worth of stock in the end, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Could’ve been much worse if Marta hadn’t taken us in and if we hadn’t spent the morning playing high-stakes fridge Tetris. Still, there’s a special pain that comes with throwing out expensive stock while knowing exactly how many services it took to prep it. You don’t need me to explain that bit. You’ve watched duck legs go in the bin before. You know the face.

Then, at 12.15, we had to 86 the panna cotta.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”, which is what happens when you combine coffee, ice cream and a kitchen that no longer has the emotional range to name dishes properly. And here’s the insulting part: people loved it. Properly loved it. More than they would’ve loved the panna cotta.

One table acted like we’d invented the whole concept that morning. Yes, sir, thank you, we specifically destroyed our coolroom so we could bring you this spontaneous Italian-inspired experience.

You spend all that time making something delicate and precise and setting it properly and checking every mould. Then you dump ice cream in a glass, pour coffee over it and everyone starts carrying on like Raff’s got a secret dessert genius locked downstairs.

Kitchens are humbling like that.

Best moment was table nine. A lady sitting near the window had apparently watched Benny and me escorting the beef shin down the laneway during the trolley incident. When her main came out she asked whether the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

Benny nearly disappeared into the pass laughing.

I told her it was locally sourced and had only travelled a very short distance. She seemed happy with that.

And then we just… did service.

That’s the stupid part, Jonno. Once the stock was moved, the ice was in, the menu had been adjusted and everybody understood there was no rescue party coming, it turned into the best service we did all year. No stuffing around. No drifting. Everybody was locked in. Calls were clear, passes were clean, people helped each other without being asked. Kev somehow kept everything moving out back while acquiring enough ice to preserve a small whale.

I’ve worked easier services that felt ten times worse. You know the ones. Everything’s technically available but everyone’s half a step behind and mildly shitty with each other. This was the opposite. Nothing was available, half our cold storage belonged to the café next door, there was a milk crate wheel lying unattended in the laneway, and the whole team was excellent.

Bistro kitchens really do run on bar fridges and spite.

As for the Cup itself, my horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad.

Yes. Ice Cold Lad.

On the day my coolroom gave up refrigeration as a concept, I drew a horse called Ice Cold Lad, and he came second last. Not even last, which at least would’ve been funny enough to win something. Second last. Completely useless. The universe had been setting that joke up since the compressor died and still fumbled the ending.

By the time we finished I was wet, tired, financially responsible for an emerging croissant crisis and owed Marta roughly my body weight in baked goods. But the food went out, the punters had a great time, and nobody at lunch had the faintest idea that their three-course set menu had been held together by borrowed fridge space, fourteen bags of servo ice and Benny dragging beef through the rain.

Actually, table nine had some idea. Respect to her.

So that’s what happened. No dramatic moral. Phil still thinks “just make it work mate” counts as leadership, Wally eventually got the part from Sydney, and I now look at undercounter fridges with the sort of affection normal people reserve for old dogs.

You would’ve cried before the first entrée went out. Then you’d have tried to claim afterwards that you were “calm under pressure”, despite all available evidence from the years we worked grill together.

Come home ya flog. I’ll buy you a pint and you can pay Marta back in croissants.
